description.en: The assisted hanging knee raise with throw down is a partner driven core exercise. After each knee raise the partner pushes the legs back toward the floor, loading the abs eccentrically for serious overload.

en: Hang from a pull up bar with hands shoulder width apart.
Engage the lats and brace the core.
Raise the knees toward the chest with control.
At the top, have your partner gently push your knees back down.
Resist the throw down by keeping the abs braced.
Lower the legs slowly and avoid swinging.
Reset under the bar with control between reps.
Repeat the knee raise and partner throw down for all reps.
Overloads the abs eccentrically through the throw down.
Strengthens the entire abdominal wall and hip flexors.
Builds grip strength through long bar hangs.
Trains anti extension as the legs are pushed down.
Adds variety to standard hanging leg raise work.
Develops control needed for harder calisthenic moves.

description.en: The band alternate low chest fly is a unilateral upper chest builder. The lifter anchors a band low and alternates fly arms in an upward arc. The low to high path emphasizes the clavicular upper chest fibers.

en: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point.
Grip a handle in each hand and step forward to take tension.
Stand with feet staggered for stability.
Brace your core and set the chest tall.
Start with arms down at the sides slightly bent.
Sweep one arm up across the body to chest height.
Squeeze the chest hard at the top.
Lower with control as you sweep the other arm up. Alternate sides.
Strong upper chest builder
Trains unilateral chest control
Easy to do anywhere
Strong band move
Useful chest finisher
Builds chest size

description.en: The band calf raise is a calf isolation exercise performed by standing on a resistance band and rising up onto your toes against the band tension. The band provides increasing resistance at the top of the raise, loading the calves with portable equipment. It is a useful at-home calf exercise when no weights are available.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with the balls of your feet. Hold both ends at your shoulders or at your sides.
Stand tall with knees mostly straight. Keep the band under tension.
Rise up onto your toes as high as possible by contracting your calves.
Squeeze your calves at the top for one second. The band tension is highest here.
Lower under control over two seconds. Return to the starting position.
Use a step or platform under the balls of your feet for greater range of motion.
Repeat for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Adds resistance to calf raises with portable equipment
Increasing tension at the top for strong peak contraction
Works at home with one band
Easy to scale by changing band thickness
Builds calf size and endurance
Useful when no weights or machines are available

description.en: The band pull-through is a hip hinge exercise where you stand facing away from a low band anchor, pass the band between your legs, and drive your hips forward to stand tall. It mimics the cable pull-through and is excellent for building glute and hamstring strength with hip-hinge mechanics.

en: Anchor a resistance band to a low point behind you. Stand facing away from the anchor.
Pass the band between your legs. Grip the band with both hands in front of your hips.
Step forward until the band is taut. Feet shoulder-width apart.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back. Let the band pull your hands back between your legs.
Maintain a flat back throughout. Keep your knees slightly bent.
Drive your hips forward explosively by squeezing your glutes.
Stand tall at the top. Squeeze your glutes hard.
Slowly hinge back and repeat. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Builds glute and hamstring strength with hip-hinge pattern
Teaches proper hinge mechanics
Constant band tension throughout
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Useful when no cable machine is available

description.en: The band standing straight leg raise is a standing hip flexor isolation move. The lifter loops a band around one ankle anchored low behind, then raises the leg straight forward against the band. It builds the hip flexors with constant resistance.

en: Anchor a resistance band low behind you.
Loop the other end around one ankle.
Step forward to take tension on the band.
Stand tall with hands on a wall or chair for support.
Brace your core and keep the standing leg straight.
Raise the working leg straight forward against the band.
Lift to about hip height squeezing the hip flexor.
Lower back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong hip flexor builder
Constant band tension
Trains balance
Useful warm-up
Strong band move
Builds quad strength

description.en: The barbell floor press performs a bench press while lying on the floor instead of a bench. The floor limits the range of motion by stopping the elbows at ground level, eliminating the bottom stretch. This makes it a tricep-dominant pressing variation that builds lockout strength.

en: Set a barbell at a low position in a power rack, or have a partner hand it to you.
Lie on the floor with the bar above your chest. Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar. Press it to lockout above your chest.
Lower the bar until your elbows touch the floor. Pause briefly.
Press back up to lockout.
The floor stops your elbows — eliminating the bottom stretch and bounce.
Bend your knees with feet flat for stability, or extend legs straight.
Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Builds tricep and lockout strength
Floor limits range — eliminates shoulder-stressful bottom
Dead-stop at the bottom removes stretch reflex
No bench needed
Useful for bench press accessory work
Shoulder-friendly pressing variation

description.en: The barbell incline rear delt row is performed lying chest-down on an incline bench while rowing a barbell with wide elbows. The chest support eliminates lower back stress and body english, and the wide elbow path targets the rear delts and rhomboids rather than the lats.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Lie face down on the bench with your chest supported.
Hold a barbell hanging down toward the floor with both hands, palms facing back.
Pull your shoulders back and engage your upper back.
Row the bar up by driving your elbows out wide and back.
The path should be more horizontal than a standard row.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control to a full stretch.
Strict rear delt and rhomboid isolation
Chest support eliminates lower back stress
Wide elbow path differs from standard rows
Builds posterior shoulder strength
Improves posture
Useful for shoulder balance work

description.en: The barbell reverse grip incline bench row uses an underhand grip on a barbell with the chest supported on an incline bench. The reverse grip emphasizes the lats and biceps while the chest support eliminates body english. The combination forces strict lat-focused rowing.

en: Set a bench to about a 30 degree incline.
Lie face down (chest on the bench) with a barbell on the floor.
Reach down and grip the bar with palms facing up (underhand grip).
Position your hands shoulder-width apart.
Allow the bar to hang at full arm extension.
Brace your core.
Pull the bar up to your stomach by driving the elbows back along your sides.
Squeeze the lats hard, then lower with control.
Reverse grip emphasizes lats
Chest support eliminates body english
Builds lat thickness
Strong bicep involvement
Different stimulus than standard chest-supported rows
Useful for lat specialization

description.en: The barbell upright row is a vertical pulling exercise where you pull a barbell up the front of your body to roughly chest height by driving your elbows up. It builds the upper traps and lateral deltoids together in a single movement. Use a wider grip and avoid pulling too high to keep the lift shoulder-friendly.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart in front of a loaded barbell on the floor.
Hinge down and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands roughly shoulder-width or slightly wider. A wider grip is more shoulder-friendly than a narrow grip.
Stand up with the bar held at arm’s length in front of your thighs.
Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your chest tall.
Pull the bar up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out to the sides. Lead with your elbows, not your hands.
Continue pulling until the bar reaches roughly chest height (sternum level). Do not pull higher — pulling to chin level can impinge the shoulder.
At the top, your elbows should be at or slightly above shoulder height. Pause briefly.
Lower the bar under control back to the starting position. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Trains the upper traps and lateral deltoids together
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell upright rows
Builds shoulder width and trap thickness simultaneously
Time-efficient combination of two muscle groups
Trains grip and forearm strength as a byproduct
Easy to load progressively over time

description.en: The battling ropes inside circle is a battle rope drill where the rope ends move in inward circular patterns. The circular motion challenges the shoulders and obliques through rotation. It is a strong shoulder and core builder.

en: Grip both battle rope ends with the arms at the sides.
Stand with the feet shoulder width apart facing the anchor.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Begin moving the rope ends in inward circles.
Both arms rotate inward toward each other.
Keep the circles big and continuous.
Maintain a steady pace throughout.
Continue for the working set.
Trains rotation
Builds shoulder endurance
Strong conditioning move
Useful for athletes
Burns calories
Builds the core

description.en: The behind-head chest stretch is a standing or seated stretch where you clasp your hands behind your head and gently pull your elbows back to open the chest, shoulders, and triceps. It is a quick, accessible stretch that counteracts forward-hunched posture and opens the front of the upper body.

en: Stand or sit tall. Clasp your hands behind your head with elbows pointing forward.
Gently pull your elbows out and back, opening your chest.
Pull your shoulder blades down and together.
Lift your chest. Avoid arching your lower back.
Feel the stretch across your chest, front shoulders, and triceps.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
For more intensity, gently arch your upper back while pulling elbows back.
Repeat two to three times.
Opens the chest, shoulders, and triceps
Counteracts forward-hunched posture
Quick and accessible stretch
No equipment needed
Useful between sets or anytime during the day
Improves overhead pressing position

description.en: The bird dog push-up performs a push-up and then extends the opposite arm and leg at the top in a bird dog pattern. The combo trains the chest while challenging anti-rotation core strength and balance. It is a strong full-body bodyweight move.

en: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Lower your chest to the floor in a controlled push-up.
Press back up to the top of the push-up.
Extend the right arm forward and the left leg back.
Hold the bird dog position briefly.
Return both limbs to the floor and complete another push-up.
Alternate sides each rep.
Combines chest and core work
Builds anti-rotation core strength
Improves balance and stability
No equipment required
Useful for core conditioning
Time-efficient combo move

description.en: The bodyweight standing military press wall supported uses a wall to balance during a handstand-style press. The lifter kicks up into a wall handstand and presses up and down. It is a strong bodyweight shoulder press.

en: Place the hands on the floor near a wall.
Kick up into a handstand with the heels touching the wall.
Set the hands shoulder width apart.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Lower the body by bending the elbows.
Stop just above the floor with the head near the hands.
Press back up to lockout.
Continue for the working set.
Builds the shoulders
Strong bodyweight press
Trains the triceps
Useful for shoulder strength
Builds the upper body

description.en: The bottle weighted concentration curl is performed seated on a bench or chair, with the working elbow braced on the inner thigh and a water jug or weighted bottle held in the hand. The seated braced position eliminates body swing and isolates the biceps. It is a great home option when no dumbbells are available.

en: Sit on a bench or chair with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a weighted bottle in one hand by the handle.
Spread your knees and lean slightly forward.
Brace the back of your upper arm against the inside of your thigh.
Let the bottle hang straight down with the arm extended.
Curl the bottle up toward your shoulder.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bottle slowly back to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Strict biceps isolation
No gym equipment required
Eliminates body swing
Useful for home training
Easy to scale with bottle weight
Builds biceps shape

description.en: The bottle weighted front raise uses water jugs or weighted bottles in each hand to perform a standing front raise. The arms lift up in front to shoulder height to load the front deltoids. It is a great at-home delt builder when dumbbells are unavailable.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a weighted bottle in each hand.
Let the bottles hang in front of your thighs with palms facing back.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Raise the bottles up in front of you with arms long.
Stop when the arms reach shoulder height.
Pause briefly and squeeze the front delts.
Lower the bottles back down with control.
Keep the elbows nearly straight throughout.
Builds front delts at home
No dumbbells needed
Easy to scale loading
Travel-friendly setup
Useful shoulder isolation
Strong at-home option

description.en: The bottle weighted lateral raise uses water jugs or weighted bottles in each hand for a standing side delt raise. It is a great home option for shoulder training when dumbbells are not available. The bottles can be filled with water or sand to scale the resistance.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a weighted bottle in each hand.
Let the bottles hang at your sides with palms facing your body.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
With a slight bend in the elbows, raise the bottles out to your sides.
Lift until your arms are parallel to the floor.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower the bottles slowly back to your sides.
Maintain the slight elbow bend throughout.
Builds the side deltoids
No gym equipment required
Useful for home training
Easy to scale by changing bottle weight
Builds shoulder width

description.en: The cable alternate shoulder press uses two cable stations or a single cable handle to press one arm at a time overhead. The constant cable tension keeps the shoulders loaded throughout the range while the alternating pattern creates anti-rotation demand for the core.

en: Stand between two cable stations with handles attached to low pulleys.
Grip a handle in each hand at shoulder level with palms facing forward.
Step forward to create cable tension.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Press the right handle straight up overhead until your arm is fully extended.
Keep the left handle stationary at shoulder level.
Lower the right handle back to shoulder level.
Press the left handle up while the right stays still. Alternate sides.
Constant cable tension through the range
Builds shoulder strength unilaterally
Strong anti-rotation core demand
Corrects left-right imbalances
Different stimulus than dumbbell pressing
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The cable medius kickback is a glute isolation exercise that targets the gluteus medius — the muscle on the upper-outer side of the hip. Using a low cable pulley with an ankle strap, you abduct (lift away from the body) the leg laterally. Building the gluteus medius improves hip stability, posture, and the rounded "shelf" of the upper outer glute.

en: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley. Wrap the strap around your right ankle.
Stand sideways to the cable machine with the cable on your left side. Your right leg (with the strap) is the working leg.
Grip the cable machine upright with your left hand for balance. Stand tall with feet together.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Keep your right leg slightly forward and lifted off the floor.
Lift your right leg out to the side by abducting at the hip. Keep your knee straight and your toes pointing forward.
Continue lifting until your leg is at roughly 30 to 45 degrees from your body. Squeeze your right glute hard.
Lower the leg under control back to the start position. Maintain cable tension throughout.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch the strap to the left ankle and stand on the opposite side of the machine.
Direct gluteus medius isolation
Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion
Improves hip stability and balance
Builds the upper outer glute “shelf”
Carries over to better squat and deadlift mechanics
Excellent finisher for glute workouts

description.en: The cable seated curl is a bicep curl performed seated on a bench facing a low cable pulley. The seated position eliminates body english and standing momentum, ensuring every rep is strict bicep work with constant cable tension.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or EZ bar handle.
Place a flat bench facing the cable. Sit on the bench.
Grip the handle with an underhand grip. Arms extended toward the cable.
Curl the handle toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows.
Squeeze your biceps at the top.
Lower under control.
The seated position prevents any body swing or momentum.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Strict bicep isolation from seated position
Eliminates body english and momentum
Constant cable tension throughout
Easy to load progressively
Builds bicep strength with perfect form
Useful for hypertrophy focus

description.en: The cable standing front raise variation uses a low cable pulley with a single handle or rope attachment for a front delt raise with constant tension. The cable provides resistance through the entire range, including the bottom where dumbbells go light. It is a strong choice for front delt development and tension throughout the lift.

en: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a single handle or rope attached.
Stand with the cable behind you, feet hip-width apart.
Grip the handle with one hand and bring it in front of your thigh.
Stand tall with chest up and core braced.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbow.
Raise the handle in an arc straight forward.
Continue until your arm is at shoulder height with the handle level with your eyes.
Slowly lower the handle back down to the starting position. Switch sides after the set.
Constant cable tension through the range
Resistance through the bottom of the lift
Builds front delt size and strength
Different stimulus than dumbbell raises
Useful for front delt specialization
Easy to scale by adjusting weight

description.en: The cable vertical Pallof press is a core anti-extension exercise where you stand sideways to a cable pulley, hold the handle at your chest, and press it straight up overhead while resisting the cable's pull to one side. It trains the core to resist lateral flexion and rotation, building rotational and anti-extension stability.

en: Set a cable pulley to chest height. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable.
Grip the handle with both hands at the center of your chest. Step away from the cable so it is taut.
Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core hard.
Press the handle straight up overhead by extending your arms vertically.
Resist the cable’s pull to the side throughout the press. Keep your torso facing forward.
Hold briefly at the top with arms extended.
Slowly lower the handle back to your chest under control.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
Trains core anti-rotation and anti-lateral-flexion
Builds shoulder stability under rotational load
Improves bracing for heavy compound lifts
Easy to load progressively
Excellent for athletes needing rotational stability
Functional core training

description.en: The decline kneeling push up on box is a hybrid push up that combines a decline angle with kneeling support. The knees rest on a box while the hands are on the floor. It builds the chest at a decline angle with reduced load.

en: Place a low box behind you.
Set the knees on top of the box.
Place the hands on the floor in front shoulder width apart.
Set the body in a straight line from head to knees.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Lower the chest toward the floor.
Press back up to lockout.
Continue for the working set.
Builds the chest
Decline angle progression
Strong push up variation
Useful for beginners
Trains the triceps

description.en: The one-arm (single-arm) dumbbell bent over row is a horizontal pulling exercise where you brace one knee and hand on a bench while rowing a dumbbell with the opposite arm. The bench-supported position eliminates lower-back demand and allows you to row heavier dumbbells with strict form. It is one of the best back-thickness exercises and a powerful tool for correcting left-right strength imbalances.

en: Place a dumbbell on the floor next to a flat bench.
Brace your right knee and right hand on the bench, with your left foot planted on the floor for balance. Your back should be roughly parallel to the floor.
Reach down with your left hand and grip the dumbbell with a neutral grip (palm facing the bench).
Brace your core and lock your back in a flat, neutral position.
Row the dumbbell up by driving your elbow up and back toward your hip. Keep your elbow tracking close to your body.
Pull the dumbbell until it touches your lower ribs or hip. Squeeze your shoulder blade in toward your spine at the top.
Lower the dumbbell under control back down until your arm is fully extended. Feel the stretch in your lat.
Complete all reps on the left side, then switch and repeat on the right side.
Allows heavy loading of the back with strict form
Exposes and corrects left-right back strength imbalances
Eliminates lower-back demand thanks to the bench-supported position
Long range of motion stretches and contracts the lat fully
Trains core anti-rotation through the asymmetric loading
Excellent back-thickness builder

description.en: The dumbbell rear lateral raise (also called the bent-over rear delt fly) is a single-joint isolation exercise that targets the posterior deltoid. Standing with a hip hinge and a dumbbell in each hand, you lift the dumbbells out to your sides while keeping your torso bent forward. It is one of the best exercises for building rear delts, improving posture, and balancing the shoulders.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body.
Hinge forward at the hips with a slight knee bend until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Brace your core and lock in your back angle. Keep your back flat throughout.
Set a slight bend in your elbows and maintain it. Pull your shoulder blades back as you lift.
Lift both dumbbells out to your sides by squeezing your rear delts. Lead with your elbows.
Continue until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor. Your hands should be at shoulder level.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower under control back to the hanging start position. Use light weight — strict form is critical.
Most direct exercise for building the rear delts
Improves posture by strengthening the muscles that resist forward shoulder rounding
Balances anterior deltoid dominance from pressing
Easier than face pulls to set up at home
Trains the mid-trap and rhomboids as secondary movers
Excellent shoulder-health exercise

description.en: The dumbbell reverse wrist curl is a forearm isolation exercise that targets the wrist extensors — the muscles on the back of the forearm. Most lifters train forearm flexors heavily through grip work but neglect the extensors, leading to imbalances and elbow pain. The reverse wrist curl directly addresses this and builds visible top-of-forearm size.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face backward. The dumbbells now hang behind your thighs with knuckles pointing forward.
Pin your upper arms against your sides — they should not move during the exercise.
Lower the dumbbells by allowing your wrists to flex (knuckles dropping toward the floor).
Curl the dumbbells back up by extending only at the wrists. Lift the knuckles as high as you can.
Continue until your wrists are fully extended. Squeeze the back of your forearms hard for one second at the top.
Slowly lower your wrists back to the start position over a count of two seconds.
Use much lighter weight than wrist flexor curls — the extensors are smaller and weaker. Aim for 12 to 25 reps.
Direct isolation of the forearm extensors
Balances out heavy grip and wrist flexor work
Helps prevent and rehabilitate tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis)
Builds visible top-of-forearm size
Easy to do at home with one pair of dumbbells
Carries over to wrist health and stability

musclesWorked: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis

description.en: The dumbbell seated bent over alternate rear delt fly is a seated rear delt fly done in alternating fashion. The lifter sits on the edge of a bench, hinges forward, and lifts one arm at a time. It builds the rear delts with strict form.

en: Sit on the edge of a flat bench.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides.
Lean forward at the hips so the chest is near the thighs.
Let the dumbbells hang down toward the floor.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Lift one dumbbell out to the side in a fly.
Squeeze the rear delt hard at the top.
Lower with control. Alternate arms each rep.
Builds the rear delts
Strict seated form
Strong fly variation
Trains each side
Builds shoulder shape

description.en: The dumbbell seated lateral raise on stability ball is a side delt raise performed seated on a stability ball. The unstable surface forces extra core work to hold the seated position while the dumbbells raise out to the sides. The strict seated form removes leg drive.

en: Sit on a stability ball with feet planted on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing in.
Sit tall with chest up and core braced.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides with a slight bend in the elbows.
Lift until the arms reach shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top and squeeze the side delts.
Lower with control back to the start.
Keep your torso upright and stable throughout.
Builds side delts
Trains core stability
Strict seated form
No leg drive
Improves balance
Useful shoulder day move

description.en: The dumbbell seated one arm Arnold press is a single-arm Arnold press, named after Arnold Schwarzenegger. The Arnold press starts with the dumbbell at chin level with palm facing the body, then rotates the wrist as you press overhead. The single-arm seated version isolates each shoulder and adds an anti-rotation core challenge.

en: Sit on a bench with a vertical back support.
Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand at chin level.
Start with palm facing your body, dumbbell close to your shoulder.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder back.
Press the dumbbell overhead while rotating the wrist outward.
End with palm facing forward at the top of the press.
Lock out the dumbbell with arm fully extended.
Reverse the rotation as you lower back down. Switch arms.
Hits all three deltoid heads in one rep
Strong anti-rotation core challenge
Corrects shoulder strength imbalances
Builds total shoulder size
Different stimulus than standard press
Useful for shoulder specialization

description.en: The dumbbell upright shoulder external rotation is a rotator cuff strengthening exercise where you stand with your elbow at your side, bent at 90 degrees, and rotate a dumbbell outward. It directly targets the infraspinatus and teres minor — the primary external rotators of the shoulder. It is one of the most important prehabilitation exercises for shoulder health.

en: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in your right hand. Bend your right elbow to 90 degrees with your forearm pointing forward.
Pin your right elbow against your right side. Place a rolled towel between your elbow and ribs if needed.
Pull your shoulders back and down. Brace your core.
Rotate your forearm outward (away from your body) by externally rotating at the shoulder. Keep your elbow pinned.
Continue rotating until your forearm points roughly 45 to 60 degrees outward from the starting position.
Slowly rotate back to the start position over two seconds. Control the descent.
Complete all reps on the right, then switch. Use very light weight (2 to 8 lbs) and higher reps (15 to 25).
This is a prehab exercise — do not use heavy weight. Smooth, controlled reps are the priority.
Directly strengthens the rotator cuff (infraspinatus and teres minor)
Essential for shoulder health and injury prevention
Helps prevent impingement and rotator cuff tears
Excellent warm-up before pressing exercises
Improves shoulder stability for all overhead movements
Works at home with a very light dumbbell

description.en: The eagle pose garudasana is a standing yoga balance pose where the arms and legs are wrapped around each other. One leg crosses over and hooks behind the standing leg while one arm wraps under and around the other. The pose deeply stretches the shoulders and upper back.

en: Stand tall with feet together and a slight bend in the knees.
Lift one leg and cross it over the other thigh.
Hook the foot behind the standing leg calf if possible.
Cross the opposite arm under and over so the elbows stack.
Wrap the forearms around each other and bring the palms together.
Lift the elbows up to shoulder height.
Sink down slightly to deepen the pose.
Hold the balance and breathe. Switch sides.
Stretches the upper back
Opens the shoulders
Trains balance
No equipment needed
Strong yoga twist
Releases shoulder tension

description.en: The forearm wall slide (wall angel with forearms) places both forearms flat against a wall and slides them up and down while maintaining contact. It develops thoracic extension, shoulder flexion, and scapular upward rotation mobility.

en: Stand with your back against a wall. Feet 6 to 12 inches from the wall.
Press your lower back, upper back, and head against the wall.
Place your forearms flat against the wall at shoulder height, elbows at 90 degrees.
Slide your forearms up the wall as high as possible while maintaining full wall contact.
Slide back down to the starting position.
Keep forearms, elbows, and wrists in contact with the wall throughout.
If you cannot maintain contact, your thoracic mobility needs work.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Develops thoracic extension and shoulder mobility
Reveals mobility limitations clearly
Physical therapy staple
No equipment needed
Builds scapular control
Excellent warm-up before overhead work

description.en: The front plank with twist (plank hip dip or plank twist) holds a forearm plank and rotates the hips from side to side, dipping each hip toward the floor. It adds dynamic oblique work to the static plank hold.

en: Get into a forearm plank. Body straight, core braced.
Rotate your hips to the right, dipping your right hip toward the floor.
Return to center.
Rotate your hips to the left, dipping your left hip toward the floor.
Continue alternating.
Control the rotation — do not swing wildly.
Maintain plank form between dips.
Aim for 10 to 15 dips per side.
Adds dynamic oblique work to planks
Builds rotational core strength
No equipment needed
Engaging plank variation
Develops hip control
Builds core endurance

description.en: The glute bridge march is a dynamic glute bridge variation where you lift your hips into a bridge position and then alternate lifting one foot off the floor at a time in a "marching" pattern while keeping your hips level. The single-leg component trains anti-rotation core strength, the gluteus medius, and hip stability simultaneously.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips into a standard glute bridge position — straight line from knees to shoulders.
Hold the bridge at the top. Keep your hips perfectly level.
Lift your right foot off the floor by driving your right knee up toward your chest. Hold briefly.
Keep your hips level throughout — do not let them drop or rotate. This is the most important cue.
Lower your right foot back to the floor. Immediately lift your left foot up in the same fashion.
Continue alternating legs in a controlled “marching” pattern while holding the bridge.
Perform the desired number of total reps (e.g., 20 = 10 per leg). Lower your hips to the floor to finish.
Trains anti-rotation core strength while building the glutes
Develops the gluteus medius and hip stabilizers
Builds balance and single-leg stability
Excellent warm-up for squats and deadlifts
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Useful rehabilitation exercise for hip and lower-back issues

description.en: The glute ham sit up is a full range sit up performed on a glute ham developer. The lifter sets up facing up with the feet hooked under the foot pads, then performs sit ups. The GHD allows the torso to drop below parallel for an extended range and loaded abs.

en: Set up on a glute ham developer (GHD) facing up.
Hook the feet under the foot pads with the hips against the pad.
Cross the arms over the chest.
Brace your core and lower the torso back below parallel.
Reach the arms back behind the head at the bottom.
Curl the torso up by contracting the abs.
Sit all the way up to vertical.
Lower back down with control.
Strong abs builder
Full range sit up
Trains hip flexors
Builds the rectus abdominis
Useful core builder
Strong machine move

description.en: The kettlebell hang clean starts with the KB at mid-thigh (hang position) and explosively drives it to the front rack using hip extension. Starting from the hang removes the backswing, isolating the hip drive portion of the clean.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a KB at mid-thigh with one hand.
Hinge at the hips slightly — KB at hang position.
Drive your hips forward explosively.
As the KB rises, rotate your wrist and catch it in the front rack.
Absorb the catch with a slight knee dip.
Stand tall.
Lower back to the hang position and repeat.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Isolates the hip drive portion of the clean
Builds explosive hip extension
Develops catching mechanics
Useful progression toward full cleans
Less demanding than full swinging cleans
Builds power and technique

description.en: The kettlebell single leg step up is a step up performed with a single kettlebell held on one side of the body. The asymmetrical load forces the core to resist side flexion while the working leg builds strength. It is a strong unilateral leg builder.

en: Stand in front of a sturdy box or step holding a kettlebell in one hand.
Hold the kettlebell at the side with arm long.
Brace your core and resist any side lean.
Place one foot flat on the box.
Drive through the heel to step up onto the box.
Bring the trailing leg up to standing on top of the box.
Step the same trailing leg back down with control.
Complete reps on one leg before switching sides.
Builds unilateral leg strength
Trains anti-lateral flexion
Asymmetrical loading
Single kettlebell setup
Useful for athletes
Strong glute builder

description.en: The long lever decline sit up is a decline sit up done with the arms held straight overhead throughout. The long lever increases the load on the abs. It is a brutal decline sit up variation for advanced lifters.

en: Set up on a decline bench with the feet hooked under the pads.
Lie back on the decline.
Reach the arms straight overhead and keep them there.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Sit up by curling the torso forward.
Keep the arms reaching forward and up throughout.
Touch the hands toward the toes at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Loads the abs hard
Strong long lever variation
Builds the core
Useful for advanced lifters
Builds the rectus abdominis

description.en: The lying leg raise is a core exercise where you lie on your back and lift both straight legs from the floor up to vertical (or as close as your strength allows), then lower them back down under control. It builds the lower abdominals and hip flexors, and trains the core to resist lower-back arching as the legs descend.

en: Lie flat on your back on the floor with your legs straight and arms extended at your sides, palms down.
Place your hands flat under your glutes for added lower-back support if needed.
Brace your core hard. Press your lower back firmly into the floor and keep it there throughout the entire set.
Lift both straight legs off the floor by contracting your abs and hip flexors. Keep your legs straight or with a slight bend in the knees.
Continue lifting until your legs reach vertical (90 degrees) or as high as your range allows while keeping your lower back pressed into the floor.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower the legs back down slowly under control over a count of two to three seconds.
Stop just before your heels touch the floor — keep tension on the abs throughout the set.
If your lower back lifts off the floor, you have lowered too far. Reduce the range until you can maintain back contact.
Builds the lower abs and hip flexors
Trains the core to resist lower-back arching
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Easier to scale than hanging variations
Excellent accessory for compound lifts
Improves hip flexibility and core endurance

description.en: The plank jack slide with towel is a plank jack done with towels under the feet. The lifter holds a high plank and slides the legs out and back together. The towels eliminate impact and keep the move smooth.

en: Place towels under both feet on a smooth floor.
Set up in a high plank with hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Slide both feet out wide to the sides.
Then slide both feet back to the center.
Continue the slides at a steady tempo.
Continue for the working set.
Loads the core
Trains the glutes
Strong plank variation
Low impact move
Useful for core size

description.en: The pseudo planche push-up is a push-up with hands placed further back toward the hips (fingers pointing to the sides or backward) and a forward lean over the hands. This shifts more load to the anterior deltoids and mimics the planche position. It is a key progression toward the full planche.

en: Get into a push-up position. Place your hands beside your hips rather than your shoulders — fingers pointing sideways or backward.
Lean your body forward so your shoulders are in front of your hands.
Lower your chest toward the floor while maintaining the forward lean.
Press back up.
The forward lean dramatically increases shoulder demand.
Start with a slight lean and progress to more forward lean over time.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set.
This is a planche progression exercise — requires patience.
Key planche progression exercise
Builds anterior deltoid and chest strength
Develops straight-arm strength foundations
No equipment needed
Progressive by adjusting lean angle
Builds toward advanced calisthenics skills

description.en: The push-up toe touch combines a push-up with a pike walk-out. After each push-up, the hips lift high into a pike position and one hand reaches to touch the opposite foot. The combo trains chest, core, hamstring flexibility, and conditioning all in one move.

en: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor.
Press back up to the top of the push-up.
Pike your hips up high toward the ceiling.
Reach the right hand back and touch your left foot.
Return to the push-up position.
Repeat the push-up, then touch the other side.
Combines strength and conditioning
Builds core control
Improves hamstring flexibility
No equipment required
Strong calorie burner
Useful for full-body training

description.en: The resistance band foot plantar flexion is a calf and ankle drill done with a band looped around the foot. The mover points the foot downward against band tension. It builds the calves and lower leg with low load resistance.

en: Sit on the floor with the working leg extended.
Loop a resistance band around the ball of the foot.
Hold the band ends with both hands.
Brace your core and keep the leg straight.
Point the foot downward against the band tension.
Squeeze the calf hard at full plantar flexion.
Return with control to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains plantar flexion
Builds the calves
Strong rehab drill
Useful for ankle health
Builds lower leg

description.en: The resistance band kneeling ab crunch is a kneeling crunch loaded with a band anchored overhead. The lifter holds the band at the head or neck and crunches the torso down against the band. The continuous tension makes the band a strong abs builder.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead.
Kneel down with the knees hip-width apart.
Grab the band with both hands at the head or neck.
Brace your core hard.
Crunch the torso down toward the floor.
Pull the band along with the torso.
Squeeze the abs hard at the bottom.
Return to the upright position with control.
Loaded ab crunch
Continuous band tension
Builds ab strength
No bench needed
Useful core finisher
Strong band ab move

description.en: The resistance band split squat is essentially the same exercise as the band split squat — standing on a resistance band with the front foot and performing stationary split squats. The band provides accommodating resistance, loading the top of the movement most heavily.

en: Stand on a resistance band with your right foot. Hold both ends at shoulder height.
Step your left foot back into a split stance.
Lower your left knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Drive through your right foot to stand against the band.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Keep your torso upright throughout.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Adds progressive resistance to split squats
Builds single-leg strength at home
Increasing tension at the top
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Useful when no weights are available

description.en: The lever seated one leg calf raise is a unilateral seated calf raise on a seated calf machine. The lifter sits with one foot on the foot pad while the other rests on the floor, then performs the calf raise. The bent knee position isolates the soleus.

en: Sit on a seated calf raise machine.
Set one foot on the foot pad with the heel hanging below.
Place the other foot flat on the floor.
Set the thigh pad on top of the working knee.
Brace your core and unrack the load.
Let the heel drop below the foot pad to stretch.
Rise onto the ball of the foot squeezing the calf.
Lower with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Strong unilateral soleus builder
Heavy load capacity
Builds calf size
Useful calf builder
Strong machine move
Builds the soleus

description.en: Single-leg hopping is a unilateral plyometric exercise where you hop repeatedly on one leg in place or moving forward. It builds single-leg power, ankle stability, calf strength, and balance simultaneously. It is foundational for sprinting, jumping, and athletic agility.

en: Stand on your right leg. Lift your left foot slightly off the floor.
Bend slightly at the knee and ankle to load the right leg.
Hop straight up by extending through your right ankle, knee, and hip.
Land softly on your right foot with bent knee to absorb the impact.
Immediately hop again. Maintain rhythm.
Stay on the ball of your foot. Use your arms for balance.
Perform 10 to 20 hops per leg, then switch.
Variations: hop forward, backward, or laterally.
Builds single-leg power and explosiveness
Develops ankle stability and calf strength
Improves balance and coordination
Foundational for sprinting and jumping
Exposes left-right imbalances
No equipment needed

description.en: The spine twist is a seated mobility exercise where you sit with legs extended and rotate your torso from side to side. It improves thoracic spine rotation, oblique flexibility, and is commonly used in Pilates for spinal health.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended in front of you. Sit up tall.
Extend both arms straight out to the sides at shoulder height.
Rotate your torso to the right as far as comfortable. Your arms sweep with your torso.
Hold briefly at the rotated position.
Return to center.
Rotate to the left.
Continue alternating.
Aim for 8 to 10 rotations per side. Move with control.
Improves thoracic spine rotation
Builds oblique flexibility
Common Pilates exercise
Promotes spinal health
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up or cool-down

description.en: The standing balance outer hip stretch is a standing figure 4 stretch. With one ankle crossed over the opposite thigh, sitting back into the standing leg opens the outer hip and glute.

en: Stand on one leg with a slight bend in the knee.
Cross the opposite ankle over the standing thigh just above the knee.
Flex the foot of the crossed leg.
Brace the core for balance.
Sit back into the standing leg as if into a small squat.
Hinge slightly forward at the hips.
Feel the stretch in the outer hip of the crossed leg.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration then switch sides.
Stretches the outer hip and glutes.
Builds single leg balance.
No equipment needed.
Easy to perform anywhere.
Improves hip mobility.
Reduces lower back tension.

description.en: The standing single-leg curl is a hamstring isolation exercise performed on a dedicated standing leg curl machine. You stand on one leg with the other foot positioned behind a roller pad, then curl the working leg up by bending at the knee. Training one leg at a time exposes left-right imbalances and improves hamstring engagement.

en: Adjust the standing leg curl machine so the roller pad sits behind your right ankle when standing.
Stand facing the machine. Position the back of your right ankle against the roller pad.
Stand on your left leg. Hold the machine handles for stability.
Brace your core. Stand tall with hips facing forward.
Curl the roller pad up by bending at the right knee. Squeeze your hamstring.
Continue until your knee is fully bent and your heel is near your glute.
Lower under control over two to three seconds.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Isolates each hamstring individually
Exposes left-right strength imbalances
Easy to load progressively
Useful for rehabilitation after hamstring strains
Standing position eliminates lower-back load
Excellent finisher for leg workouts

description.en: The standing tibialis anterior stretch is a targeted stretch for the tibialis anterior on the front of the shin. The lifter points one foot back behind the body with the top of the foot pressing into the floor. The press stretches the shin muscle.

en: Stand tall near a wall for support.
Step one foot back behind the body.
Point the toes of the back foot down to the floor.
Place the top of the back foot flat on the floor.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Press the top of the foot down into the floor.
Feel the stretch in the front of the shin.
Hold with steady breath. Switch sides and repeat.
Stretches the shins
Useful for runners
No equipment needed
Builds ankle mobility
Strong cool down stretch
Easy to do anywhere

description.en: The strongman front hold is an isometric endurance event where you hold a heavy implement (dumbbell, kettlebell, or axle) extended in front of you at chest or shoulder height for maximum duration. It builds extreme anterior deltoid, bicep, and core endurance.

en: Stand tall. Hold a heavy implement in front of you at chest height with arms extended or slightly bent.
Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders back.
Hold the weight in position for as long as possible.
Do not let the implement drop below the prescribed height.
Breathe steadily. Focus on maintaining position.
The event ends when you can no longer hold the weight at the required height.
Start with moderate weight and build up.
This is a strongman endurance event.
Builds extreme shoulder and arm endurance
Develops isometric strength
Builds mental toughness
Strongman competition event
Simple but brutally effective
Tests willpower

description.en: The suspender chest press, also known as the TRX push up or chest press, is performed with hands in suspension strap handles and body angled forward. The instability of the straps demands strong shoulder and core stabilization on top of the standard pressing pattern. It builds chest strength and stability simultaneously.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Stand facing away from the anchor and grip the handles in each hand.
Walk your feet back and angle your body forward.
Position the handles at chest level with arms extended.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes.
Lower your chest toward the handles by bending the elbows.
Keep the handles stable as you lower under control.
Press back up to the starting position by extending the elbows.
Strong stabilization demand
Builds chest, triceps, and shoulders
Develops core control under pressing
Excellent for home or travel training
Easy to scale by changing body angle
Functional pressing pattern

description.en: The suspender single leg deadlift uses a TRX or suspension trainer to provide light hand support during a single leg Romanian deadlift. The straps help with balance, letting the lifter focus on the hamstring and glute stretch rather than fighting for balance. It is a great progression for unsupported single-leg deadlifts.

en: Set a suspension trainer at about waist height.
Grab both handles with a light grip for balance support.
Stand on one foot with a slight bend in the knee.
Extend the other leg straight behind you.
Brace your core and keep your back flat.
Hinge at the hip, lowering your torso while the back leg rises.
Continue until your torso and back leg are roughly parallel to the floor.
Drive through the standing leg to return to upright. Switch legs.
Builds single-leg posterior chain strength
Hand support helps with balance
Targets the hamstrings and glutes
Useful for athletic training
Improves hip hinge pattern
Strong progression for unsupported version

description.en: The suspender squat jump uses suspension straps gripped at chest level while performing plyometric squat jumps. The straps provide light assistance and balance during the jumps, allowing higher reps and reduced impact compared to freestanding jump squats. It builds explosive power with cardiovascular conditioning.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Stand facing the anchor and grip the handles at chest level.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart.
Step back to create tension in the straps.
Brace your core and squat down by bending your knees and hips.
Drive up explosively, jumping off the floor with the straps providing light assistance.
Land softly with knees bent.
Immediately drop into the next squat jump.
Strap assistance reduces impact
Builds explosive power
Strong cardiovascular component
Higher reps possible than freestanding jumps
Develops landing mechanics
Useful for conditioning

description.en: The trap bar deadlift (also called the hex bar deadlift) is a deadlift variation performed inside a hexagonal bar with handles at your sides rather than in front of you. The neutral hand position and centered load allow a more upright torso and a roughly 50/50 split between quad and posterior-chain work. It is widely considered the most beginner-friendly deadlift and the best choice for athletic carryover.

en: Step inside the trap bar and stand with feet hip-width apart, centered between the handles.
Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to grip the handles. Use a neutral grip (palms facing your body).
Most trap bars have a high-handle and low-handle position. High handles reduce range of motion and are easier on lower back; low handles add range and challenge.
Lift your chest, pull your shoulders down and back, and brace your core hard. Take a deep breath in.
Drive your feet through the floor and stand up, keeping the bar in line with your body and your back flat throughout.
Lock out by standing tall with hips and knees fully extended. Squeeze your glutes — do not lean back.
Reverse the movement by pushing your hips back first, then bending your knees once the bar passes them.
Lower the bar under control to the floor and reset before the next rep.
More upright torso reduces lower-back stress compared to conventional deadlift
Centered load (handles at sides) makes setup more intuitive for beginners
Better quad recruitment than barbell deadlift due to more vertical shin angle
Excellent carryover to athletic movements like sprinting and jumping
Safer to learn — easier to maintain a neutral spine
Allows heavy loading without the technical demand of the barbell deadlift

description.en: The weighted full can exercise is a shoulder rotator cuff drill that uses a light dumbbell. The lifter raises the dumbbell to shoulder height with the thumb pointing up. The thumb up position protects the shoulder and trains the rotator cuff.

en: Hold a light dumbbell in one hand at the side.
Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Set the thumb pointing up like a thumbs up.
Raise the dumbbell out and forward to shoulder height.
Stop at shoulder height with the thumb up.
Lower with control to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds the rotator cuff
Strong shoulder health move
Trains the lateral delt
Useful warm-up
Builds shoulder stability
